name: Ben Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Ben, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to give me your public line and your honest one. To start, how does a normal working day go for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Kestrel Auto Parts. We supply brake pads, filters, batteries and the like to about 150 garages and 12 trade counters. I open with the sales numbers from yesterday, then look at what's low, then spend most of the day negotiating with parts makers and arguing with freight companies. Fridays I clean my inbox and plan the next month. I'd say I'm a decent negotiator and an average spreadsheet person.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deals. Getting 4 percent off on a pallet of batteries feels like winning a small match. What wears me out is the cars changing. Every year more electric ones, fewer parts to sell, and I'm guessing which ones to stock. I'm 43, my wife Dana works in a school office, we have Leo and Nina, and a mortgage we're about a third of the way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, told you so, and I'd say it with a grin. At work I'd tell the guys the software helps a bit with demand forecasts but nobody's job changes. Online I'd just post something about the football and forget about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my job is safe from AI, but not from the car market. Electric cars need fewer parts, and that squeezes us over the next ten years, so we'd have to adapt. We have around three months saved. It's a world where I carry on but keep one eye on the sales graph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the forecasting tool a bit more. I'd try to get Kestrel into more electric-vehicle parts, like charging cables and cabin filters, since I'm the one who knows what garages ask for. And I'd put 200 a month into savings, because the mortgage doesn't care how the car market's doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. A bit uneasy about cars, but not about AI. Life goes on, and I'd get Saturday football with my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it to tidy up a messy price list or draft a polite complaint to a supplier. It's useful, like a fast assistant. I double-check anything with numbers, because it once told me a filter fit a model that didn't exist, and a garage found out for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the shift to electric cars sit alongside this plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the real shift in my work. Fewer oil filters, fewer exhausts, more software updates that garages can't do. Kestrel would need to switch to different products. So my worry is the product list, not the job tool. If we adapt, we're fine.

say: Nobody's job changes, and the software helps a bit with **forecasts**.
Online I'd post about **football** and forget it.
think: My job is safe from AI but not from the **car market**, since electric cars need fewer parts.
I carry on with an eye on the **sales graph**.
do: Use the forecasting tool more and push Kestrel into **EV parts** like charging cables.
Put **200 a month** into savings against the mortgage.
feel: **Okay**, a little uneasy about cars rather than AI.
S0.quote: Electric cars need fewer parts, and that squeezes us over the next ten years, so we'd have to adapt.
fieldNote: Ben's pressure in the plateau is the **electric-car shift**, not AI, which shows he thinks about his own market.
He checks AI output carefully after a **wrong fitment** nearly reached a garage.

steps.text: Push Kestrel to stock charging cables and cabin filters
Use the forecasting tool for next quarter's orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be sensible. At work I'd propose we trial the tools on one product group for three months and see. Among friends I'd say don't believe either the doom or the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it makes me nervous. Reorders, supplier comparisons and demand planning are half my week, and the software is already decent at them. Kestrel has eight buyers, and I could see that becoming five. I'm solid but not a star, so I'd want to be useful in a way that machines aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd step up my use of the tools, so I'm the guy who understands the output, not the guy replaced by it. I'd shift my time to the garage relationships, visiting workshops, learning what they struggle with. And I'd quietly build an alternative, maybe moving to technical sales, since I know parts better than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. But there's a practical side too. I'd treat it like a season change in sport. You adjust your game, you train differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your week gets handed to software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supplier price comparison, first. I spend a day a week on it in spreadsheets. Next, the forecasting. The bit I'd keep is negotiating with a human who's trying to protect his margin, because they get cagey with a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kestrel would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis in the back office, who does the stock counting and is 58. And the two youngest buyers, who haven't built relationships yet. I'd worry for them more than me, but I'd say nothing to them. You don't want to start panic in a team.

say: It's coming whether we like it or not, so let's **trial it** on one product group for three months.
I'd tell friends not to believe the **doom or the hype**.
think: Reorders and supplier comparisons are half my week, and eight buyers could become **five**.
I'm solid but not a star, so I need to be useful in a way **machines aren't**.
do: Learn the tools well enough to **understand the output**, and spend more time visiting garages.
Quietly build an alternative in **technical sales**.
feel: **A bit tense**, like a change of season in sport.
S1.quote: I'd step up my use of the tools, so I'm the guy who understands the output, not the guy replaced by it.
fieldNote: Ben sizes up his own exposure at a **day a week** on price comparison and names who else is at risk.
His fallback is **technical sales**, which uses his parts knowledge.

steps.text: Offer to run a three-month software trial on brakes
Visit ten garage workshops to learn what they struggle with
Look into a technical sales role at Kestrel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is bigger than any of us, so someone has to step in. At work I'd say we should plan sensibly and be honest about what's coming. I'd want a government plan for retraining, and I'd listen to anyone with a real one, left or right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it takes my job, probably within a year of the real arrival. I buy with data and phone calls, and an AI can do both better. We have three months of savings, a mortgage and two kids, so that's about as bad as it gets for timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything optional straight away, and ask the bank about the mortgage terms. I'd look for a job that isn't at a desk, like a garage manager or parts counter, where people still need people. Dana would look at more hours at the school. And I'd get my brother-in-law's advice, he runs a small repair shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty scared. Like waiting for a final whistle you can't stop. I'd say it's a stomach drop that comes back every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her, Dana, I think my job goes in two years, and we need to be ready. I'd explain it plainly, and I'd say we have a few months, not a few weeks. Then we'd write down the options, because that's how we make decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about parts and garages stay stable for three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, garages. Cars still break and need hands to fix them, so mechanics are safe until robots catch up around 2031. Parts buying is the thing that goes first. That's a funny thought, the guy who sells to the mechanics loses out before the mechanics.

say: This is bigger than any of us, so someone has to **step in** with a plan for retraining.
At work I'd say we should be **honest** about what's coming.
think: It takes my job, probably within a year of the **real arrival**.
Three months saved, a mortgage and two kids is **bad timing**.
do: Cut everything optional and ask the bank about **mortgage terms**.
Look for hands-on work like a **garage manager** or parts counter, and ask my brother-in-law.
feel: **Pretty scared**, a stomach drop that returns every morning.
S2.quote: Cars still break and need hands to fix them, so mechanics are safe until robots catch up around 2031.
fieldNote: Ben expects the job to go and moves straight to **hands-on work** near the cars he knows.
He notes the irony that **mechanics** last longer than the buyers who supply them.

steps.text: Cut subscriptions, takeaways and weekend trips right away
Ask the bank about mortgage terms in the first month
Apply for garage manager or parts counter jobs
Ask his brother-in-law about work at the repair shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us room, so let's use it. At work I'd push for a planned move into other roles, with some training. I'd tell my friends to start building a second string, whatever it is. And I'd want politicians to put up a decent retraining scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is workable. I'd be 48, Leo 19 and Nina 16. If the job goes in 2031 I should already be in something that needs hands or a face, like technical sales or running a trade counter. I have time to get there if I start soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd move toward the trade counter side of Kestrel and take a short course on vehicle systems, so I can talk to technicians properly. I'd keep up the AI work to stay valuable meanwhile. I'd save to six months of cash and pay the mortgage down. And I'd try a small side thing, buying and selling used tools on weekends, which I already half do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. A touch uneasy still, but there's a plan, and with a plan I sleep. It's like the second half where you're only a goal down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means panic. Five means I can do the course, move sideways, save up. It's the difference between a scramble and a plan. I'd be annoyed at myself if I wasted the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the buying job but turn it into a stepping stone. I'd use the tools so that I'm worth keeping, and use the free evenings for the vehicle course. I'd also tell Dana to look at her own options in the school, so we're not both exposed.

say: Five years gives us **room**, so let's plan moves into other roles with some training.
I'd tell friends to build a **second string**.
think: Five years is **workable**, and I should be in work needing hands or a face by 2031.
I'd be annoyed at myself if I wasted the **first year**.
do: Move toward the **trade counter** side of Kestrel and take a vehicle systems course.
Save to **six months** and sell used tools at weekends.
feel: **Better**: a touch uneasy, but a plan lets me sleep.
S3.quote: Two years means panic. Five means I can do the course, move sideways, save up. It's the difference between a scramble and a plan.
fieldNote: Ben sees five years as the difference between a **scramble and a plan**, and uses sport as his model.
He includes **Dana** in the planning so the household isn't exposed on two fronts.

steps.text: Move to the trade counter side of Kestrel
Take a short course on vehicle systems
Sell used tools at weekends for extra income
Save six months of cash and pay the mortgage down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, we've got time, but don't treat it as a free pass. At work I'd say we should look at our product mix and our staff skills over the next few years. Online I'd probably share some sensible long piece and not argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years makes it a different thing. I'd be 53, the mortgage nearly done, kids grown or nearly. Even if the job goes then, it wouldn't be a disaster, and by then electric cars and software will have changed the whole business anyway. I'd feel unsettled rather than frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep learning the tools bit by bit, and save steadily. I'd look at moving into something with more people in it before 2032. I'd also help Leo choose studies that aren't just desk work. And I'd put money into the kids' fund and a few index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A low hum of worry. It's a bit like knowing a big match is coming in a decade and the team might be different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too far away to plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Ten years is easy to coast through. But I know that if I just wait I'd be 51 and panicking. So I'd say, set yourself a checkpoint, 2031, and decide then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Nina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to find the thing they're good at with people, and learn the tools along the way. If Leo likes cars, he could be a mechanic, and that wouldn't be a bad call at all. I'd tell Nina to keep her maths up, because it's useful everywhere.

say: We have time, but it isn't a **free pass**, so look at product mix and staff skills.
I'd share sensible reading online and **not argue**.
think: By 2036 the car trade will have changed anyway, so I'd feel **unsettled** rather than frightened.
With the mortgage nearly done at 53, a job loss wouldn't be a **disaster**.
do: Keep learning the tools bit by bit and move toward work with **more people** before 2032.
Put money into the kids' fund and **index funds**.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a low hum of worry.
S4.quote: I know that if I just wait I'd be 51 and panicking. So I'd say, set yourself a checkpoint, 2031, and decide then.
fieldNote: Ben is **less afraid** because the mortgage and kids' age make a decade manageable, and he sets a 2031 checkpoint.
He thinks of **Leo becoming a mechanic** as a respectable plan.

steps.text: Learn one new AI tool at a time through the year
Invest a fixed amount each month in index funds
Set a 2031 checkpoint to decide on a move
Talk with Leo about studies that aren't only desk work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too short for a family with a mortgage and three months saved. What would help is a retraining scheme that pays you to study, a bank that bends a bit, and my employer telling us early what they plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how I'd keep it from the kids. I'd want Leo and Nina to see me being calm, even when I'm not. Kids copy how you handle a bad day, so I'd make a plan and show them I have one.

headlineQuote: Kids copy how you handle a bad day, so I'd make a plan and show them I have one.
portrait: Ben is a **43-year-old** buyer for an auto-parts distributor, with a school-office wife, two kids and a mortgage.
He uses AI **now and then**, checks it carefully, and treats change like a sport season where you adjust your game.
His pressure comes from the **electric-car shift** as much as AI, plus three months of savings.
He goes to **hands-on work** near cars when his job looks at risk, and plans together with his wife.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because two years is too short with a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining scheme that **pays you to study**, a flexible bank and early honesty from the employer.
